The upside-down A is the universal quantifier, read **for all** or "for every". The backwards E is the existential quantifier, read **there exists**. So ∀x ∃y Loves(x, y) reads "for every x there exists a y such that x loves y": everyone loves someone, but each person can pick a different someone. ∃y ∀x Loves(x, y) reads "there exists a y such that for every x, x loves y": one single person is loved by everyone. Same symbols, same predicate, but the first quantifier binds the outermost variable, so it decides who gets to choose. In the first, the y is chosen after the x. In the second, the y is fixed first and has to work for every x.

[[GIST]] for-all then exists, versus exists then for-all

It's a recipe for the running time of merge sort, read as "time on n items equals time on two half-size problems, plus linear work." The 2T(n/2) is the **two recursive calls** on each half of the list, and the Theta(n) is everything done outside them, like splitting and merging. Picture the recursion as a tree: it has log n levels, and each level does a total of about n work, so you get **n log n** overall.

[[GIST]] recurrence reads as two halves plus linear work

The n/2 is the size of each of the two halves. When merge sort runs on n items, it doesn't recurse on all n again, it splits the array into two pieces and sorts each one separately. If you cut n items down the middle, that's two chunks of n/2 each.

That's exactly what the 2T(n/2) records: the T says "same problem, smaller input," the n/2 says how much smaller, and the 2 in front says how many of those smaller problems there are. So it's one call on the left half plus one call on the right half, and each half has n/2 items.

Then when those halves come back sorted, the + Theta(n) is the merge that stitches them into one sorted list of n.

[[GIST]] n/2 is each half's size

The lecturer is right, and here's the full chain so it's clear where those two limits come from.

Start with the definition:

f'(x) = lim(h→0) [sin(x+h) − sin(x)] / h

Expand sin(x+h) with the angle addition formula:

sin(x+h) = sin x cos h + cos x sin h

Substitute and group the terms:

= lim(h→0) [sin x cos h + cos x sin h − sin x] / h
= lim(h→0) [sin x (cos h − 1) + cos x sin h] / h
= sin x · lim(h→0) (cos h − 1)/h + cos x · lim(h→0) sin h / h

Now the two limits. The first is 0, the second is 1, so:

f'(x) = sin x · 0 + cos x · 1 = cos x

The intuition for the two limits: sin h / h → 1 because for small h, sin h ≈ h (the arc and its chord nearly coincide). And (cos h − 1)/h → 0 because cos h ≈ 1 − h²/2, so the numerator shrinks like h² while the denominator shrinks like h.

[[GIST]] sin(x+h) expansion gives the two limits

A result that's unlikely under the null is evidence against it, but the chance the drug actually works depends on the prior and the study's power, which is why you'd need a Bayesian posterior to say something like that.

That's a common misreading, and it's worth correcting. The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme **if the null hypothesis were true**, not the probability that the null is true. So 0.03 means: assuming the null holds, a result this extreme would show up about 3 percent of the time. [[GIST]] p-value is P(data | null), not P(null)

Conditional probability is what you get when you stop asking about the whole world and ask about one slice of it. P(A|B) means the probability of A, given that you already know B is true. Formally you shrink the sample space down to just the cases where B holds, then ask what fraction of that slice A occupies, which gives P(A|B) = P(A and B) / P(B).

Rearranging that gives P(A and B) = P(A|B)P(B). The same joint probability can be written the other way round, P(A and B) = P(B|A)P(A). Set the two equal and divide by P(B):

P(A|B) = P(B|A) P(A) / P(B)

That's Bayes' theorem. The P(A) on the right is your **prior**, what you believed before seeing B. The P(B|A) is how well B is predicted by A, often called the likelihood. The P(A|B) on the left is your updated belief. For the denominator, P(B) = P(B|A)P(A) + P(B|¬A)P(¬A), since B has to happen either alongside A or alongside not-A.

Now the screening example. A disease with 1% prevalence, so the prior P(D) is 0.01. The test catches 99% of true cases, so P(+|D) = 0.99. It correctly clears 95% of healthy people, so the false positive rate P(+|¬D) is 0.05. The overall positive rate is then 0.01 × 0.99 + 0.99 × 0.05 = 0.0099 + 0.0495 = 0.0594. So P(D|+) = 0.0099 / 0.0594 ≈ 0.167, about 17%, or one in six.

The concrete version: out of 10,000 people, 100 have the disease and 99 of them test positive. Of the 9,900 who don't, 495 get a false positive. So you have 594 positives, and only 99 are real.

The mistake people make most is **base rate** neglect, also called the transposed conditional: reading P(+|D) as P(D|+) and concluding a positive means a 99% chance of disease. The test is accurate; the disease is just rare, and rarity is what drags that 99% down to 17%.

[[GIST]] prior times likelihood over evidence

The key idea is that confessing is a **dominant strategy**: it gives each prisoner a better outcome regardless of what the other does. If the other stays quiet, confessing gets you a lighter sentence. If the other confesses, confessing still beats staying quiet. So rational self-interest drives both to confess, and they land on an outcome that's worse for both than mutual silence. That gap between individual rationality and collective good is the dilemma.

"Repeat it forever" is the setup for the **iterated prisoner's dilemma**: the same game played over and over with the same partner, where each round's choice can respond to what came before. That changes the logic, because a player can now reward cooperation or punish defection in later rounds, so confessing is no longer automatically dominant. The classic result is that a simple tit-for-tat strategy, cooperate first and then copy the other player's last move, tends to do well, and cooperation can become stable even though the one-shot game pushes both toward confessing.

[[GIST]] repetition makes cooperation sustainable

Cartels are a real-world repeated game, and the same tension applies. Members agree to restrict output and keep prices high, but each one has a short-term incentive to cheat by producing a little more and grabbing extra profit. In a one-shot round, cheating wins. Over time, though, the others can detect it and retaliate by flooding the market, which collapses the price for everyone. So cartels hold together only while members value the future profits of cooperation more than the quick gain from defecting, and they tend to break down when that future looks short or uncertain, when cheating is hard to detect, or when there are many members to monitor.

[[GIST]] cartels cheat, retaliation collapses them

Short answer, it solves to **Θ(n log n)**. Here's the recursion tree, level by level.

1. At the top, one problem of size n costs c·n.
2. The next level splits into 2 problems of size n/2, and those still add up to c·n.
3. The level after has 4 problems of size n/4, which again totals c·n.
4. At depth k you have 2ᵏ problems of size n/2ᵏ, and the work per level stays c·n.
5. Halving stops when the subproblem size reaches 1, so n/2ᵏ = 1 gives k = log₂ n.

So there are log₂ n + 1 levels, each costing c·n, which gives c·n(log₂ n + 1). Drop the constants and it's **Θ(n log n)**. The master theorem gives the same thing faster: a = 2 and b = 2, so log_b a = 1, and since f(n) = Θ(n) matches n¹ exactly, you're in the case that tacks on an extra log factor.

[[GIST]] tree sums to n per level

Simplest version: a heap's leaves are already heaps, and in the 1-indexed layout the leaves all sit after index floor(n/2). So you only need to fix the nodes above them, and you go right to left, bottom up.

For n = 7, that's index 3. Sift-down means: look at a node and its two children, and if a child is smaller, swap it up, then keep going down from there. Why it's **O(n)** and not **O(n log n)**: most nodes are near the bottom, so they can only drop a little. Add up how far each node can move and the total grows in step with n, not n times log n.

[[GIST]] leaves already heaps, total work grows linearly

A shift happens when something other than price changes, like income, tastes, or the price of a substitute. Then **the whole curve moves**, so at every single price people now want more or less than before. Tea doubling in price would shift the coffee demand curve right.

So the test is simple: did the good's own price change? Then it's a movement. If anything else changed, it's a shift.

The key constraint is that I can't hold the whole grid, so I can't do a normal flood fill. What I can do is track connectivity between the current row and the previous one, since islands only connect vertically between adjacent rows.

So I keep two rows in memory: the previous row and the current one. For each row, I label the runs of ones, then union any run in the current row with an overlapping run in the previous row. I maintain a union-find over the active labels, and when a label's last cell has passed and it can no longer connect downward, I finalize it and increment the count. That gives me the island count in one pass with memory proportional to the width of a row, not the height.

The tricky part is the union-find bookkeeping: I need to know when a component is truly closed so I don't double count it, and I need to handle a run that merges two previously separate components. That's the part I'd be careful about.

[[GIST]] stream rows, union-find across adjacent rows

## Approach
Count each element's frequency with a hash map, then keep the top k. The cleanest way is a bucket sort: index buckets by frequency, so bucket f holds every element that appears f times. Walk the buckets from highest frequency down and collect until you have k elements, which avoids sorting all distinct values.

## Code
```python
from collections import Counter

def topKFrequent(nums, k):
    counts = Counter(nums)
    buckets = [[] for _ in range(len(nums) + 1)]
    for num, freq in counts.items():
        buckets[freq].append(num)

    result = []
    for freq in range(len(buckets) - 1, 0, -1):
        for num in buckets[freq]:
            result.append(num)
            if len(result) == k:
                return result
    return result
```

## Complexity
Time is O(n), one pass to count and one pass over the buckets. Space is O(n) for the counter and the bucket array.

I haven't run Postgres in production myself, but I'd partition it, yes. Range partition by time on the event timestamp, monthly or weekly, so vacuum and autovacuum work per-partition instead of one huge table, and old partitions can be dropped instead of deleted.

What gets harder: cross-partition queries and unique constraints need the partition key, planning gets more complex, and you have to manage partition creation and retention as automation.

A heap is the other standard way to do it, and it's the one I'd reach for when I can't afford the O(n) bucket array, say when the counts are huge or the input is a stream. I keep a min-heap of size k keyed by frequency, push each element, and pop the smallest whenever the heap grows past k. That gives O(n log k) time and O(k) space, which beats the bucket approach on memory when k is small relative to n. I went with buckets here because the counts are bounded by n, so it's linear, but the heap is the more general tool.

[[GIST]] heap trades O(n) for O(n log k)

`enumerate` gives you `(index, char)` tuples, so `ch` is a tuple, never a character, and `right` is never defined. On `"abcabcbb"` the first iteration stores `seen[(0,'a')]` and crashes on `right`. Unpack it, and only jump `left` when the repeat is inside the current window:

```python
def length_of_longest_substring(s):
    seen = {}
    left = 0
    best = 0
    for right, ch in enumerate(s):
        if ch in seen and seen[ch] >= left:
            left = seen[ch] + 1
        seen[ch] = right
        best = max(best, right - left + 1)
    return best
```

The `seen[ch] >= left` check stops a stale index from outside the window from pulling `left` backwards.

[[GIST]] unpack enumerate, guard left

Goroutines are multiplexed onto OS threads by the Go runtime scheduler, which is an M:N scheduler. Each goroutine starts on a logical processor, a P, and each P is bound to an OS thread, an M. The runtime keeps a local run queue per P plus a global queue, and when a goroutine blocks on a syscall or a channel operation, the scheduler parks it and runs another one on that thread, or hands the P off to a different thread so the work keeps moving. Work stealing balances the queues across Ps.

For channels versus mutexes: I reach for a channel when I'm passing ownership of data or coordinating a sequence of events between goroutines, and a mutex when I'm just protecting a shared piece of state that multiple goroutines read and write. A mutex is simpler and cheaper for guarding a map or a counter, and a channel is the better fit for pipelines, fan-out, and signaling.

Use Floyd's tortoise and hare: move a slow pointer one step and a fast pointer two steps until they meet, which proves a cycle exists. If they never meet, the list is acyclic. Once they do meet, reset one pointer to the head and advance both one step at a time; the node where they meet again is the start of the cycle.

For a feed that's constantly getting new inserts, offset pagination breaks because the offsets shift under you. I'd use **keyset pagination** on a stable, unique sort key. Since events are newest first, I'd sort by a monotonic column like a timestamp plus a tiebreaker, usually the event id, and the cursor encodes the last row's sort key. The next page is just "where sort key is less than the cursor," so inserts at the head never shift what you've already seen.

The tiebreaker matters because timestamps collide. If two events share a timestamp, ordering by timestamp alone can skip or repeat rows, so the composite key of timestamp and id makes the order total and stable. I'd also make the cursor opaque, base64 of the encoded key, so clients can't hand-craft it and I can change the internals later.

One caveat: if events can be backfilled with older timestamps, keyset still holds as long as the sort key is immutable. If a row's sort key can change, that's the case where you'd need a snapshot or a versioned cursor instead.

[[GIST]] keyset pagination on timestamp plus id

Walking through **"abba"** with the corrected code:

1. Index 0, char `a`: not seen before, so the window becomes `"a"` and best is 1.
2. Index 1, char `b`: new, so the window is `"ab"` and best becomes 2.
3. Index 2, char `b`: it was last at index 1, so **left jumps to 2**, the window is just `"b"`, and best stays 2.
4. Index 3, char `a`: `a` was last at index 0, which sits **behind the current left** of 2, so we ignore it, the window is `"ba"`, and best stays 2.

The function returns 2. The interesting step is the last one: without the `seen[ch] >= left` guard, that stale index 0 would drag left back to 1, giving a window of `"bba"` and a wrong answer of 3. The guard keeps left from ever moving backwards.

For 2, 7, 11, 15 with target 9, the answer is indices 0 and 1, since 2 + 7 = 9.

The approach I'd use is a hash map in one pass. For each number, I check whether its complement, target minus the current value, is already in the map. If it is, I return the stored index and the current one. Otherwise I store the current value with its index and keep going. That avoids the brute-force double loop.

Time complexity is O(n), since each element is inserted and looked up once. Space is O(n) for the map in the worst case.

I haven't built a double-entry ledger directly, but I've worked on the idempotency side of it. At Quillfeather I migrated 38 cron scripts into a single Temporal-based scheduler, which removed a whole class of double-send bugs, so I've dealt with exactly the retry problem you're describing.

For the design: an accounts table with a type and a normal balance, and a ledger_entries table where each entry has a transaction_id, account_id, direction, amount, and a running balance. Every payout writes two entries that sum to zero, debit the escrow or payable account, credit the grower's account, all inside one transaction.

For the retry guarantee, I'd put a unique idempotency key on the payout, so a retried request hits the constraint and returns the original result instead of writing new entries. The key is generated once when the payout is created, not per attempt, and the whole thing runs in a single database transaction so the entries and the key commit together.

I led Project Tern, a rewrite of our carrier-settlement service from a Rails monolith into three Go services. We split it because settlement had three genuinely different workloads: rate quoting, event ingestion, and reconciliation. Rate quoting was read-heavy and latency-sensitive, so I cut its p95 from 820 ms to 190 ms with a batched loader and a 90-second Redis cache keyed by lane ID. Ingestion ran through Dockhand, a Kafka pipeline handling about 2.3 million shipment status events a day, with a transactional outbox so we never wrote a duplicate. Reconciliation was a nightly job comparing carrier invoices against booked loads, which took monthly mismatches from 312 down to 41. On the cutover, the outbox and idempotent writes were what kept us from paying a carrier twice.

For example two, grace is zero, so windows only merge when they touch or overlap. [5, 10] and [10, 12] touch at 10, so they merge into [5, 12]. The next window starts at 13, and the gap from 12 to 13 is one minute, which is bigger than grace 0, so it stays separate. That gives [[5, 12], [13, 20]].

For example three, grace is 1, so that same one-minute gap now falls within the merge threshold. [13, 20] merges in, and the result is [[5, 20]]. The key point is that grace only decides whether windows merge, it never extends the end. So the merged window ends at 20, the largest end among the windows it absorbed, not 21.
